conversation.content:
Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Claire, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. Today we’re going to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way for us to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days and see what kind of support might help you feel more like yourself again.

Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety, and even then we’ll work together on next steps. We’ll go through ten questions; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about numbers or labels. We’ll take it at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification anytime.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Good morning… I, um, I’m not sure. I still smile when the baby does something cute—like yesterday when she wrapped her tiny hand around my finger—but even those moments feel kind of… muted? Like I can tell it’s sweet, but the warm rush I used to get isn’t really there. I still watch my shows and try to scroll through funny videos while I nurse, but they don’t pull me in the way they did before she was born. So I guess the enjoyment hasn’t totally disappeared, it just feels flatter, like someone turned the volume down.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I still laugh sometimes, mostly when my partner makes goofy faces at the baby or when the dog tries to “check on” us during diaper changes. But the laughter feels quick, like it fades right away, and I don’t get that light feeling afterward. I’ll chuckle and then almost immediately feel tired again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself stuff like, “Tomorrow we’ll go for a walk to the park,” and I think I should feel excited about getting out of the house. But when the time comes, it just feels like another chore—packing the diaper bag, wondering if she’ll cry the whole way. So, no, I can’t really say I’ve been looking forward to much. Even coffee with a friend I used to count down the days for now feels… meh. I’ll still go, but it’s more to not feel isolated than because I truly expect to enjoy it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah… like the other night she wouldn’t settle for two hours straight, and I kept thinking maybe I ate something at dinner that upset her stomach, or I hadn’t burped her long enough. My partner said she was just having “one of those evenings,” but I still felt it must’ve been something I missed. It’s not every little thing—just every now and then I catch myself replaying what I did or didn’t do.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s sleeping soundly in the bassinet, and suddenly my chest feels tight like something bad’s about to happen—even though nothing’s wrong. I check if she’s breathing, wonder if the room’s too warm, too cold, if she’s gaining enough weight, if that tiny cough means she’s getting sick. I know most of it’s probably normal-mom stuff, but the feeling just pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Um… not really full-on panicky. I do get this sudden wave of “what if I can’t handle this?” sometimes—like when she cries and I can’t figure out what she needs—but it’s more of a quick rush than a real panic attack. My heart races for a minute, then I force myself to breathe slow and it passes. I wouldn’t say I’m scared out of the blue, just those flashes of worry that maybe I’m in over my head.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finally get her down for a nap, think I have a minute to shower, and the washer buzzes or the dog needs out and it just piles up. I don’t fall apart, but by evening I’m snapping at my partner over tiny things because everything feels like “one more thing.” I keep telling myself I should be able to juggle it all better.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m up crying or anything, but I do lie there with my mind racing—going over the next feeding, wondering if she’ll wake up in ten minutes, replaying every little thing I did that day. Some nights I fall asleep okay, then snap awake for no reason and can’t drift off again. It’s not every night, maybe three or four times this week, but it leaves me even more wiped the next day.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of down, off and on. It’s not there every minute—when she smiles I get a little lift—but it’s like a gray cloud that keeps drifting back in. I’ll catch myself tearing up while folding laundry, thinking “Is this really my life now?” Then I feel guilty because I love her so much. So yeah, I’ve been sad, just not all-day-every-day hopeless.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No, I haven’t actually cried much. A couple of times my eyes have welled up—like when she wouldn’t latch and I felt completely useless—but the tears never quite spilled over. Mostly I just feel this heavy ache in my chest instead of actually crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get overwhelmed, sure, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and even on the worst nights I know I have to stay here for her.

I hear how hard you're trying to stay afloat right now: enjoying your baby's tiny smiles yet feeling as though every pleasure is turned "down low," worrying about every little detail even when nothing is wrong, and ending most days exhausted yet snapping at those closest to you. You're doing your absolute best to care for your daughter while a persistent gray cloud of low mood, racing thoughts, and self-doubt hovers in the background.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, framing even formerly pleasant outings as burdensome chores and using "meh" to convey emotional flatness</sym>, <sym>Patient reports occasional self-blame that persists despite reassurance, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, frequent, intrusive worries that occur "a few times a day" without external triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and inability to keep up with daily demands, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes racing-thought insomnia 3-4 nights in the past week, waking after initial sleep and being unable to return to sleep, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent but not constant low mood, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 17 places you well above the 14-point threshold that signals probable major <med>depression</med> with <med>peripartum onset</med>. Core criteria emerge in your report: diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>) nearly every day (<quote>the warm rush I used to get isn't really there</quote>), low mood (<quote>a gray cloud that keeps drifting back in</quote>), sleep disruption, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness (<quote>I should be able to juggle it all better</quote>), and difficulty concentrating due to racing worries-all present most days for the past two weeks. Anxiety items are also highly endorsed, consistent with comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. Q10 score of 0 indicates no current self-harm risk. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and if necessary <med>sertraline</med> or other <med>SSRI</med> medications compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these EPDS results with your partner and build a daily support plan-e.g., scheduled rest blocks, household task delegation, and 15-minute "you-time" while a trusted adult watches baby
4. Begin simple self-care: four-square breathing when chest tightness hits, limit evening screens, keep bedroom dark and cool, and aim for a 20-minute outdoor stroll each morning light to help reset sleep-wake cycle
5. Arrange practical help now-friends dropping off meals, grocery delivery, or a postpartum doula-to lower daily stress load
6. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress; if thoughts of self-harm ever develop, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note  

**Presenting Symptoms / Behavioral Observations**  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” intermittent tearfulness  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal anticipatory pleasure; activities feel obligatory)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt when infant is fussy  
- Unprompted, recurrent worries about infant’s well-being; physical anxiety (chest tightness)  
- Episodic “rush” of overwhelm/self-doubt, mild autonomic arousal, no frank panic attacks  
- Sleep disruption related to intrusive, racing thoughts; middle-of-night awakening 3–4×/week  
- Global sense of “treading water”; irritability when extra demands arise  

**Pattern Summary**  
Mood and anxiety symptoms present most days, interfere with enjoyment and rest, no functional impairment in caregiving, no self-harm ideation.  

**Screening Significance**  
Meets provisional threshold for possible **minor-moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety**; scores would likely fall within “at-risk” range on EPDS. Continue monitoring, consider fuller assessment with standardized tool, review supports/stressors, and evaluate need for stepped-care intervention.  

**Safety**  
Denies thoughts of self-harm; no current safety concern.
